cues.en: Stockoverflow says you must use smart pointers. The handmade hero code base has no smart pointers. How can this be? So roughly what I would say about that is you can imagine, if you imagine like a programmer's life cycle, it looks something like the following.
cues.zh: Stack Overflow 上说你必须用智能指针。但 Handmade Hero 的代码库里却没有智能指针。这怎么可能呢？对此我大致想说的是，你可以想象一下，如果把程序员的成长轨迹画出来，它大概长这个样子。

cues.en: You know, no one's like just a born knowing how to program. It's something that you learn. And inside your brain, you learn to program in very definitely in stages, right? And the stages are pretty consistent, I think. And so we won't like, I won't try to, you know, do them all here. But
cues.zh: 你知道，没人是天生就会写代码的。这是后天学来的。在你的大脑里，学习编程的过程绝对是有阶段性的，对吧？而且我认为这些阶段还挺规律的。所以我们不用……我不打算在这儿把所有阶段都列出来。但是，

cues.en: at some point when you go through these stages you get to stage N and stage N is I guess what I would call the individual element thinking, right? Individual element thinking is when you think of each specific piece of data in your code as having its own lifetime.
cues.zh: 在某个时刻，经历过这些阶段后你会来到阶段 N，阶段 N 大概就是我所说的“孤立元素思维”，对吧？所谓的孤立元素思维，就是你认为代码中的每一块具体数据都有它自己的生命周期。

cues.en: Um, so for example, if you're going to create like an R code, we have entities. You think about every entity as getting like a new or a malloc or, you know, the first time you create it. And then you think of it having like a, an end point that it's its own. And that's where you call like delete or the garbage collector, you know, cleans it up.
cues.zh: 额，举个例子，就像在我们代码里要创建实体。你觉得每个实体在第一次创建时，都要走一遍 new 或者 malloc 之类的。然后你觉得它有一个专属的终点，在那个地方你会调用 delete，或者由垃圾回收机制来把它清理掉。

cues.en: or a smart pointer in this case automatically deletes it because someone else is owning it or whatever, right? And these architectures tend to look like they have like RAII style. They have like, you know, literally like thousands or millions of new delete, you know, or malloc free. They have
cues.zh: 或者在这种情况下由智能指针自动删除它，因为有别的东西拥有它之类的，对吧？这类架构往往看起来很有 RAII 风格。它们会有，你知道，成千上万个 new delete，或者 malloc free。它们会有

cues.en: giant nests of pointers from things to other things, right? And this is just some place you get to in your thinking about how this is like with respect to architecture, right? Now, a lot of people never move past this point.
cues.zh: 各种对象之间互相指向的巨型指针嵌套，对吧？这只是你在思考代码架构时，认知会达到的一个阶段，对吧？然而，很多人永远都没能跨过这个阶段。

cues.en: Sometimes they don't move past this point because they never program in a language that doesn't have a garbage collector. If you're always in a language with a garbage collector, you probably don't think about these things very much. And to the extent that you ever actually will, it will only be because you're trying to do something performance oriented and you have to start pretending you're actually managing your own memory even though the garbage collector is. And most people who write games in garbage collected languages have had to do this, but if you're just doing things
cues.zh: 有时他们没能跨过这个阶段，是因为他们从没用过没有垃圾回收的语言编程。如果你一直用带垃圾回收的语言，你可能根本不会去多想这些事。如果哪天你真的开始考虑了，也仅仅是因为你在做一些偏重性能的事情，不得不开始假装自己在亲自管理内存，哪怕实际上还是垃圾回收在管。大多数用带垃圾回收的语言写游戏的人都不得不这么做过，但如果你做的

cues.en: that are not like performance critical in that way, you wouldn't know. You'd never have to get past here, right? Someone on the Twitch said, try to catch, and I'll put that in here as well. So this is individual element thinking, and it's something everyone does. I've definitely had a period where I was programming that in. So I don't want to say that people who do it are stupid or something, because
cues.zh: 不是那种对性能极其敏感的事情，你就不会懂。你也永远不必跨过这个阶段，对吧？Twitch 上有人说 try-catch，我也把它归到这一类里。这就是“孤立元素思维”，每个人都会经历这个阶段。我当年写代码也绝对经历过这个时期。所以我不是说这么做的人就很蠢什么的，因为

cues.en: Everyone does it, like there's no not doing it. I don't know anyone who ever successfully avoided this stage of thinking. The stage is stupid, meaning the code you write will be stupid, but you are not stupid because everyone does this at some point. The key is you have to get to n plus one at some point, which is group thinking, right?
cues.zh: 每个人都会这样，根本避不开。我没见过有谁能成功跳过这种思维阶段。这个阶段本身很蠢，意味着你写出的代码会很蠢，但你并不蠢，因为每个人在某个时期都会这样。关键在于，你必须在某个时刻迈向 N+1 阶段，也就是“群体思维”，对吧？

cues.en: And at group element thinking stages, this tends to be like large collections created, destroyed at the same time. You know, almost no, very, very few new delete malloc free. Heavy use.
cues.zh: 在按组思考元素的阶段，这往往像是大量集合同时创建、同时销毁。几乎不，非常非常少用 new、delete、malloc、free。大量使用。

cues.en: of scratch space. Typically like hashes and reuse show up in here a lot. So when you're talking about making this jump, when you make this jump from n to n plus one, so smart pointers live here, right? So at the stage when you're doing, when you're still stuck thinking about individual pieces,
cues.zh: 暂存空间。通常哈希和复用会在这里大量出现。所以当你说要完成这个跳跃，当你从 n 跳到 n+1 时，智能指针就处在这个阶段，对吧？所以在这个阶段，当你还在、还卡在思考单个部件时，

cues.en: all having their own lifetimes. The problem that you run into is that there's so many of these things. I mean, there's literally millions or even billions of them in a program. If you were to manually always be allocating and freeing all these things individually, you can see why people say, well, you've got to use smart pointers because otherwise you have to remember
cues.zh: 它们各自拥有自己的生命周期。你会遇到的问题是有太多这种东西。我的意思是，一个程序里真的有数百万甚至数十亿个。如果你总是手动逐个分配和释放所有这些东西，你就能理解为什么人们说，嗯，你必须用智能指针，否则你就得记得

cues.en: to always in two places. You declare the pointer and then in the destructor you have to add a delete manually. You can see why people think in their head smart pointer makes sense here because it's a way of typing something. I can just look at one line that's the declaration of the pointer and know that it's going to get automatically freed, right? Now the problem with this is you're really just patching over a flaw in your architecture.
cues.zh: 总要在两个地方处理。你声明指针，然后在析构函数里还得手动加一个 delete。你就能理解为什么人们脑子里觉得智能指针在这里有道理，因为它是一种给东西标注类型的方式。我只要看一行，也就是指针的声明，就知道它会被自动释放，对吧？但这样做的问题是，你其实只是在修补架构里的一个缺陷。

cues.en: If two things are inextricably linked such that you have one get automatically freed when the other one is freed, in all but the very, very rarest of circumstances, what that means is those things should actually have a combined lifetime. And so what should actually happen is you should have just had one large pool that all of those things got created in that is just streaming into that pool so that you'd never have to do that.
cues.zh: 如果两个东西密不可分，以至于一个释放时另一个会自动释放，那么除了极其极其罕见的情况之外，这意味着这些东西实际上应该有一个合并的生命周期。所以真正应该发生的是，你本来就该有一个大池子，所有这些东西都在里面创建，只是不断流入这个池子，这样你就永远不必那样做。

cues.en: The pool gets freed together so you don't need to have this rat's nest of pointers that you crawl through to make sure you eliminate everything. So that's what we do in Handmade Hero. We just have pools that get freed at the right time and everything that goes together goes in the pool. So I never have to sit around running around grabbing pointer.
cues.zh: 池子会一起释放，所以你不需要这团乱麻般的指针，还得爬过去确认把所有东西都清掉。这就是我们在 Handmade Hero 里做的。我们就是有在正确时机释放的池子，所有该一起的东西都放进池子里。所以我从来不用坐在那儿到处跑着抓指针。

cues.en: you know, which is what a smart pointer chains, that's what they do. One person gets free to cross, the next person gets free to cross, the next person gets free to cross, right? It's extremely inefficient. And so you're just wasting the user's time by dynamically discovering the scope of a group that you should have already known, right? So basically, when you move from here to here, smart pointers become irrelevant. You really don't need them anymore.
cues.zh: 你知道，智能指针链做的就是这件事。一个释放了，轮到下一个；下一个释放了，再轮到下一个，对吧？这极其低效。所以你只是在浪费用户的时间，去动态发现一个你本来就该知道的组的范围，对吧？所以基本上，当你从这里走到这里，智能指针就变得无关紧要了。你真的不再需要它们了。

cues.en: Because you just don't have ownership concerns like the kind that you have here. You could say ownership is a constant concern and mental overhead. Whereas here ownership is obvious and trivial in 99% of cases.
cues.zh: 因为你根本不需要像在这里一样操心所有权问题。可以说，所有权会带来持续的顾虑和心智负担。而在这里，99% 的情况下所有权都一目了然、微不足道。

cues.en: Right. So basically like the thing to understand here is just that all of the advice you see online pretty much is for people thinking at this level, which is not where you want to be. Like you're going to have to go through it at some point to understand what's going on, but your goal is to go from here to here. So advice like use smart pointers or the Rust borrow checker, like all that stuff.
cues.zh: 对。所以基本上要明白的是，你在网上看到的大多数建议，几乎都是给停留在这一认知层级的人准备的，但这绝不是你想达到的状态。虽然你某个阶段必须经历它才能搞懂是怎么回事，但你的目标是从这里跃升到更高维度。所以像什么使用智能指针或者 Rust 借用检查器这类的建议，全是那一套。

cues.en: Those are for people who are still not very good at programming, right? They're in a stage of architecture that is very limited and not appropriate for modern, high-performance, well-architected code. It's an old way of thinking that just still is very prominent, and you're just seeing advice from that. The goal is to move on.
cues.zh: 这些建议是给那些编程水平还不怎么高的人看的，对吧？他们所处的架构阶段非常局限，根本不适用于现代、高性能且架构良好的代码。这是一种依旧大行其道的陈旧思维方式，你看到的也只是基于这种思维的建议。真正的目标是超越它。

cues.en: So don't waste a lot of time learning all of this crap. You will have to go through this stage because everyone does eventually. But the goal is to get out of it as fast as you can because 100% of all code written in this style sucks. There is no such thing as a good piece of code that has these ideas in it because they are inherently inefficient, buggy, and over-architected. They're just not good.
cues.zh: 所以别把大把时间浪费在学这些垃圾玩意儿上。你确实得经历这个阶段，毕竟大家最终都得走这一遭。但目标是要尽快脱离它，因为用这种风格写出的代码 100% 都是垃圾。融合了这些理念的代码根本就没有好的，因为它们生来就低效、多 bug 且过度架构。它们就是不行。

cues.en: So this is what you're looking at. And so it's hard to discern when you see advice like this, you're like, where is it coming from? And what does it mean? That's what it means. It means that people are in this land and this is where they live. And until they move from end to end plus one, they're going to constantly be thinking things like RAII or smart pointers are good, but they're just not. They're just lousy architecture. And when you move past them, you notice immediately. You're like, oh, wow.
cues.zh: 这就是你所面对的现状。所以当你看到这种建议时很难去分辨，你会想：这到底是从哪来的？代表了什么？答案就在这儿。这意味着这些人就处于这个水平，并以此为生。除非他们能完成层级跃迁，否则他们就会一直觉得 RAII 或智能指针之类的东西很好，但其实根本不是。它们只是糟糕的架构。等你超越了它们，你立刻就会发觉。你会惊呼：“天呐，

cues.en: actually all of that crap that I used to have to spend time dealing with is just gone now. Does that help? SunCoder says n plus two is when you've reached guru stage after 30 years and your code finally looks as simple as written by someone at n minus three but is free of all the BS. You're absolutely right. Like basically my code now looks a lot like my code from
cues.zh: 原来我以前不得不花时间应付的那些破烂玩意儿，现在全都不见了。”这样解释有帮助吗？SunCoder 说，到了 n+2 阶段，也就是历经 30 年达到大师级别时，你的代码终于看起来像 n-3 水平的新手写的那样简单，但却完全摒弃了所有的狗屁设定。你说得太对了。基本上我现在的代码看起来就很像我

cues.en: 20 years ago minus a few very critical stupid things, right? But it's hard to get there. That's why I say like, you know, I try not to be too derogatory to people who talk about these things because it was me, right? The temptation is once you know that something is stupid to say that someone who does it is stupid, but it's important to remember that you were also stupid, right?
cues.zh: 20 年前的代码，只是剔除了一些致命的愚蠢问题，对吧？但要达到这一步很难。所以我才说，尽量不要去贬低那些还在谈论这些东西的人，因为我也曾是其中一员，对吧？诱惑在于，一旦你知道某件事很蠢，就会忍不住说做这件事的人很蠢，但一定要记住，你自己曾经也一样蠢，对吧？

cues.en: So, you know, stupid is as stupid does, right? So, like, I've done all this stuff, and so I know that you go through that stage. So I can't say, like, don't do this, it's stupid, because actually everyone will do this at some point. cues.zh: 你知道，傻人就做傻事，对吧？我自己这些事都干过，所以我知道你会经历那个阶段。所以我不能说“别这么做，这很蠢”，因为实际上每个人某个时候都会这么做。我想说的是，看，这是我们都会经历的阶段，这不是个好主意，所以目标只是尽快……

cues.en: past it as soon as your brain is capable of grappling with what's actually going on, right? You can think of a similar thing as like, it's like the scope of your thinking has enlarged. So at this point, your brain is only capable of focusing on like a very small piece of code. So obviously it has to think in terms of things like RAII or pointer nests.
cues.zh: 尽快走出来——只要你的大脑能应对实际发生的情况，对吧？你可以想成类似的东西，就像你的思考范围扩大了。所以在此时，你的大脑只能专注于很小一块代码。所以显然它只能用 RAII 或指针嵌套之类的方式来思考。

cues.en: Because you can only think of like this little piece. It's just it's one of the also reasons I think people like oop is Because it allows you to think very small You're just thinking about a little small piece and not how the whole program works, right? And as you can get even just a little bit larger, so maybe you're not at like the whole system yet But you're a little bit larger and now you're thinking of systems of of the in the code
cues.zh: 因为你只能想到这么一小块。这也是我认为人们喜欢 OOP 的原因之一，因为它让你能想得很小。你只想着小小一块，而不是整个程序如何运作，对吧？而当你哪怕能想得大一点，也许你还没到整个系统的层面。但你稍微大了一点，现在你思考的是代码中的各种系统。

cues.en: then you can move out to like, oh, actually, these things flow and bind together, right? And when your brain can get there, then you can just throw all this away because now you never need it anymore, right? And you're up to here, right? Does this stuff apply to game engine programming only or also to corporate logistics? It's true for all code. It has nothing to do with the type of code you're writing. Your code is always better if you think about things in terms of groups.
cues.zh: 然后你可以再往外走，哦，实际上这些东西会流动、会绑定在一起，对吧？当你的大脑能到那一步，你就可以把这些全扔掉了，因为你现在再也不需要它了，对吧？你就到这一层了，对吧？这些只适用于游戏引擎编程，还是也适用于企业物流？对所有代码都成立。跟你写的是什么类型的代码毫无关系。如果你按组来思考，你的代码总是更好。

cues.en: that work together as opposed to thinking in terms of pigeonhole elements, right? So yeah, and I'm not sure about the nn plus one, like, series thing. Like, I don't know if it's possible to teach someone in a way that makes them skip n all together. It might just not be, right? It might be that you, like I said, it's a scope issue. Like, your brain has to start thinking of the fundamental unit as not being little micro
cues.zh: 让它们协同工作，而不是按孤立的格子式元素来思考，对吧？所以是的，我也不确定那个 n+1 之类的系列说法。我不知道能不能用某种方式教人，让他直接跳过 n。可能根本不行，对吧？也可能就像我说的，这是个范围问题。你的大脑必须开始把基本单元看成不是小小的微……

cues.en: allocations, right? Because the individual element thinking is about micro allocations, right? It's about lots of little tiny things that get allocated and deleted that all have dependencies on each other. And the benefit of that is that your brain only has to think about the one tiny thing when it writes it, right? And that's why you see like what I would sort of call like, there's there's a separate thing in stage and there's like this paranoia too. It's like,
cues.zh: 分配，对吧？因为按单个元素思考就是关于微分配，对吧？它关心的是大量极小的东西被分配、被删除，而它们彼此之间都有依赖。这样做的好处是，写的时候你的大脑只需要想那一个微小东西，对吧？这就是为什么你会看到那种我会称之为……阶段里有个单独的东西，而且还有一种偏执。就像，

cues.en: It's like a person in a room with a tinfoil hat where they're trying to guard against every possible thing that could happen to this type at any time. And people think they're doing good programming when they do that, but it's actually the opposite. If you are trying to prevent errors that by the structure of your architecture cannot happen, you are literally creating worse code.
cues.zh: 就像一个人待在房间里戴着锡箔帽，试图防范这个类型在任何时候可能发生的每一件事。人们这样做时以为自己是在做好编程，但实际恰恰相反。如果你试图防止那些根据你的架构结构根本不可能发生的错误，你实际上是在写出更差的代码。

cues.en: code only should do the minimal number of things that it has to do to do the job. Anything else is just like ruining the environment, right? You are literally just expending entropy into the environment to melt the ice caps. That's all you're doing, right? There is nothing clean about code with 57,000 try-catch statements and 50 million objects just to open a file.
cues.zh: 代码应该只做完成任务所必需的最少事情。除此之外无异于破坏环境，对吧？你简直就是在向环境中散发熵来融化冰川。你干的就是这事，对吧？写了57000个 try-catch 语句、创建了5000万个对象就为了打开一个文件，这种代码一点也不干净。

cues.en: It's actually terrible and never should be done because it's a tremendous amount of CPU code spent to do absolutely nothing. The reason that people do that is because when you have this pigeonhole view and you can only program or think about this tiny little thing, all you can do is write a file handle. That's the only thing that you're working on and you refuse to consider the rest of the system at all.
cues.zh: 这其实很糟糕，根本不该这么写，因为这耗费了大量的 CPU 指令，却什么有用的事也没干。人们之所以这么做，是因为当你目光狭隘、只能编写或思考眼前这一点点小东西时，你所能做的就只有写个文件句柄。那是你唯一在忙活的事，你根本拒绝去考虑系统的其余部分。

cues.en: What else can you do? If your programming problem is by definition that you cannot work on anything larger, then paranoia, of course, sets in because anything could be true now. You have no preconditions, no post-conditions. You don't even have during conditions. You don't even know that the things that you're calling, they might throw exceptions, they might do whatever, right? And so when you start doing that,
cues.zh: 那你还能怎么办？如果你在编程上被限制为只能处理这么微小的事情，那肯定会陷入被害妄想，因为现在任何情况都可能发生。你没有前置条件，没有后置条件，甚至连执行中条件都没有。你甚至不知道调用的东西会不会抛出异常，或者干出什么别的事，对吧？当你开始这么做时，

cues.en: What you've basically decided to do is spend almost 100% of your time not actually working on the problem you were paid to solve and rather spend 100% of your time solving problems you don't actually have and creating problems for the people upstream because now all of this uncertainty is injected into the system. And so it's not that if you are doing this kind of architecture, it's not that RAI isn't necessary.
cues.zh: 你基本上就决定了：把你几乎百分之百的时间，都花在不去解决付钱让你解决的问题上，而是百分之百地去解决你根本没有的问题，并且给上游人员制造麻烦，因为现在整个系统都被注入了这种不确定性。所以如果你采用这种架构，并不是说 RAII 没必要。

cues.en: it actually is because you've actually made very bad decisions about how to structure your code such that now you really could fail at any time because you're doing a million allocations. Any one of them could fail. If instead you had just allocated as a block, now you never need any of that error handling because either it succeeded or it failed once and now you don't need to worry about all these little micro allocations, right?
cues.zh: 它其实确实必要，因为你做出了非常糟糕的代码架构决策，导致你现在随时随地都可能崩溃，因为你搞了成百万次的内存分配。其中任何一次都可能失败。反之，如果你只是整块分配，现在你根本不需要任何那种错误处理，因为它要么一次成功，要么一次失败，你现在完全不必担心所有这些零碎的小分配，对吧？

cues.en: If I allocate a block that stores a complete data structure in all the pieces, I only have one thing to check when I start. Did I get it or didn't I? If instead I allocate each little individual piece and wire them all together, every single allocation is a failure point. So now it's not paranoia to go, I need all these try accept blocks and exceptions. No, that's true now, because you've chosen a very poor way to structure your code.
cues.zh: 如果我分配一块内存来存放包含所有部分的完整数据结构，我一开始只需要检查一件事：拿没拿到？反之，如果我分别分配每个小碎片并把它们串在一起，那么每一次分配都是一个故障点。所以此时你想着“我需要所有这些 try-except 块和异常”，就不算被害妄想了。不，它成真的了，因为你选了一种非常糟糕的代码组织方式。

cues.en: So now you created all of these problems that you must now solve, right? So the key is stop thinking that way. Instead of thinking, I have to create a million little tiny things that conspire to produce a result, start thinking about what are the minimal number of resource requests I can issue to do the entire thing I need to do.
cues.zh: 所以现在你制造了所有这些必须由你来解决的问题，对吧？因此关键在于别再那么思考了。不要去想“我必须创建一百万个细小的东西来拼凑出一个结果”，而是开始去想“为了完成我需要做的整件事，我能发出的最少资源请求是多少”。

cues.en: And once you do that, you find that everything actually becomes mostly trivial. All this stuff, right? So I can tell you a simple example of a step from N to N plus 1. So when I did the first version of the characterization system at RAD, I still was at stage N. And when I did the second edition, I moved to N plus 1. And the small step I took at that time,
cues.zh: 一旦做到这一点，你会发现一切其实基本都变得很简单。所有这些，对吧？我可以给你一个从 N 到 N+1 的简单例子。我在 RAD 做第一版角色系统时，还处在 N 阶段。做第二版时，我前进到了 N+1。当时我迈出的那一小步，

cues.en: the first step was going, hey, if I have something like a character that has a certain number of bones and a certain number of meshes, right? What it used to do is I used to like knew a character and then I would knew an array of bones and I would knew an array of meshes and then the meshes would array vertices, right? All I did in that first step was I just said, oh,
cues.zh: 第一步是，嘿，如果我有一个角色，它有一定数量的骨骼和一定数量的网格，对吧？以前的做法是，我 new 一个角色，然后 new 一个骨骼数组，再 new 一个网格数组，然后网格里还要有顶点数组，对吧？我在第一步所做的只是说，哦，

cues.en: Actually, when I create a character, I made this little thing that allowed me to say, here's all the memory that I need. I need this many meshes, this many bones, this many that, this many this for the character. And I just had a little utility function, utility struct I wrote that allowed me to like say, here's the stuff I need, go. And it would then try to allocate that entire block of memory that would be needed for the whole thing. And it would parcel it out so that it would like set the pointers properly automatically for me.
cues.zh: 实际上，创建角色时，我做了个小东西，让我能说：这是我所需要的全部内存。这个角色需要这么多网格、这么多骨骼、这么多这个、这么多那个。我写了个小工具函数、工具结构体，让我可以说：这是我要的东西，开干。然后它会尝试一次性分配整个东西所需的整块内存，再把它切分好，自动帮我正确设置指针。

cues.en: That changed five, six, seven, eight failure points into one failure point, which is way more reliable, right? Just that one step makes it eight times less likely that your code will fail, that you have a bug somewhere, right? And so it's just a case of just like start wherever you can. Anything you can do in your code base to make less...
cues.zh: 这把五、六、七、八个失败点变成了一个失败点，可靠多了，对吧？就这一步，就让代码失败、某处出 bug 的概率降低了八倍，对吧？所以关键就是，从你能下手的地方开始。在你的代码库里，任何能减少……

cues.en: calls or operations that can fail, right? Just try to start collapsing them together. And eventually, right, you get to the point where you've got like the typical thing that me and John Blow do now, and I think DICE does this too, so even with the EA games do this, is every frame you just have an arena for that frame of memory, and anything that's specific to the frame just goes in there. This eliminates literally like
cues.zh: 可能失败的调用或操作，对吧？试着开始把它们合并起来。最终，对吧，你会达到一种状态，就像我和 John Blow 现在做的典型做法，我觉得 DICE 也这么做，甚至 EA 的游戏也这么做：每一帧都有一块专属于该帧的内存区域，任何该帧特有的东西都放进去。这实际上消除了……

cues.en: thousands to hundreds of thousands of allocations that happen in the kinds of systems that don't think this way. Just that one thing. And it removes almost all possible failure points because in general you can put a bound on that number and know that like as long as you can exceed that arena with a certain amount of memory you'll always be fine. So you can even base you can basically say like look this is just fine now. We literally got rid of all those failure points.
cues.zh: 在那些不这么思考的系统里，会发生的数千到数十万次分配。就这一件事。它移除了几乎所有可能的失败点，因为通常你可以给这个数量设个上界，并知道只要那个区域里有一定量的内存够用，你就永远没问题。所以你甚至可以基本说：看，现在这就没问题了。我们真的把所有那些失败点都干掉了。

cues.en: Whereas if each of those things had been a new, any single one of them could technically fail, right? Because you don't even really know, right? You have no way of even guessing how much memory that thing requires because you have no way to even measure it. But once you group them together, it's trivial to say, okay, we've looked at the peak or whatever and we just have it, right? And off we go. Steps I take now that are past that are I just design out the failure entirely.
cues.zh: 但如果其中每一项都单独 new 一次，理论上任何一个都有可能失败，对吧？因为你甚至根本不知道，对吧？你完全没法预估那玩意儿需要多少内存，因为你甚至都没办法去测量它。但一旦把它们打包在一起，事情就很简单了：好，我们看一下峰值什么的，直接分配好就行了，对吧？然后就能直接跑了。我现在采取的更进一步的做法，是直接把失败的情况从设计中彻底抹除。

cues.en: So what I do is I take arenas now and I stream into them and if they can't get more memory to grow when they need to, all the code is usually written to handle when something comes back. It just produces a stub rather than a real one and all the code still works. So that's the way I do those things now and they literally can't fail. Even if you run out of memory in the middle of something that you don't even know what the size should be, it's still just
cues.zh: 所以我现在的做法是用 arena，然后往里面流式写入；如果它们在需要扩容时拿不到更多内存，所有的代码通常都被写成能够处理返回结果的状态。它只会生成一个存根而不是真正的对象，而所有的代码依然能正常运转。所以我现在就是这么处理那些事情的，它们在字面意义上根本不可能崩溃。即使你在处理某个连大小都不知道的东西中间耗尽了内存，它依然只是

cues.en: works in the sense that it doesn't crash. It just can't draw like the rest of the things. You know what I mean? I've been concerned at all with secure coding concepts to cover undefined behavior with people looking to exploit it. So, I mean, that's a separate thing. I'm talking about failure cases that are natural, right? So, I'm not even talking about adversarial failure, right? Adversarial failure is completely different. That's like hardening.
cues.zh: 能正常跑，意思就是它不会崩溃。只是没法像其他部分一样把剩下的画出来而已。你懂我意思吧？我也一直在考虑安全编码的概念，以覆盖那些可能被恶意利用的未定义行为。不过，我的意思是，那是另一码事。我现在谈论的是自然发生的失败情况，对吧？所以我甚至不是在说对抗性的故障，对吧？对抗性故障完全是另一回事，那属于系统加固。

cues.en: However, as with all things, it is much easier to harden code written in the grouped way than it is to harden code in the individual way. Because again, if every single thing you call, if every single thing you do allocates does a new allocation, it's very hard to make any statements about bounds or where things are or when they come into existence or not.
cues.zh: 然而，和其他事情一样，对采用聚合方式编写的代码进行加固，要比对逐个分配的代码进行加固容易得多。因为话又说回来，如果你调用的每一个细小环节、你做的每一件事都在进行单独的分配，你就很难对边界、东西在哪里、或者它们何时产生做出任何确切的推断。

cues.en: It's very hard to keep that safe because it's just a sprawling mess of pointers that point everywhere, right? Whereas if everything uses IDs and an arena, it's way harder for an adversary to crack in there and it's way easier for me if I have to go harden it for some reason because like it's something that's going to get exposed to a net area or whatever to work with. So I would say n plus one makes it way easier to harden as well.
cues.zh: 要保证它的安全性非常困难，因为它就是一团到处乱指的指针乱麻，对吧？但如果所有东西都使用 ID 和 arena，攻击者就很难攻破它；而且如果出于某种原因——比如要暴露给网络区域什么的——我必须去加固它，处理起来也会容易得多。所以我认为 n+1 模式也会让代码加固变得容易得多。

cues.en: But I'm not talking about that right now. I'm strictly talking about just failures that happen normally, right? So failures that happen without an adversary. And just to be clear, like usually what I do is I use growable arenas. So I don't allocate them up front. They're like the ones in Handmade Hero now. They just grow as necessary. So basically like you just keep pushing on to the end of the arena and you have two choices for how you want to handle your failures.
cues.zh: 但我现在谈的不是那个。我严格讨论的只是正常发生的失败，对吧？也就是在没有攻击者的情况下发生的失败。而且说明一下，我通常的做法是使用可扩容的 arena。所以我不会预先全部分配好。它们就像现在 Handmade Hero 里的那种，只在需要时扩容。所以基本上你只要一直往 arena 的末尾压入数据就行了，至于怎么处理失败，你有两种选择。

cues.en: The way I like to handle failures is I just like, if you fail to push something, you just get a stub back, right? Because I don't want to have to check those for Grovel arenas. So you just get a stub back, that's all zeroed, right? And then, when you actually run through your performance, what you usually want to do then is
cues.zh: 我处理失败的方式是，如果你 push 某个东西失败，就直接拿回一个桩，对吧？因为我不想在 Grovel arena 里还得检查这些。所以你只会拿回一个桩，全是零，对吧？然后，当你真正跑性能的时候，通常你想做的是

cues.en: Each arena has an initial allocation size that you usually tune to try and make it so that it doesn't have to really do growing very often, right? Because any time you've got this system in place, you get another huge bonus, which is allocation is like very cheap. It's like one check and one add to like move the thing forward, right?
cues.zh: 每个 arena 都有一个初始分配大小，你通常会调整它，尽量让它不需要经常扩容，对吧？因为只要这套系统到位，你还会得到另一个巨大的好处：分配非常便宜。基本上就是一次检查加一次加法，把指针往前推，对吧？

cues.en: So you can also get a huge speed boost by then just looking and saying how big should these arenas be in general and setting their initial sizes to that because then you also don't hit the actual allocator almost ever, right? Let's say I want to push some dynamic amount of data and I run out of space. The calling code expects n bytes and will write n bytes, but I don't have n bytes. How do you handle this case in that style? You've got two choices.
cues.zh: 所以你也可以通过直接看：这些 arena 一般应该多大，然后把初始大小设成那个值，从而获得巨大的速度提升，因为这样你几乎永远都不会碰到真正的分配器，对吧？假设我想 push 一些动态大小的数据，然后空间用完了。调用方代码期望 n 个字节，并且会写入 n 个字节，但我没有 n 个字节。用这种风格你会怎么处理这种情况？你有两个选择。

cues.en: So one choice is that you actually write your code to look at what comes back and handle it, right? And that's still the end class way. I usually do that though. And the reason for that is because it's usually actually not that hard to do, right? I tend to check those things anyway, but you can decide not to do that. What you can do if you'd like is you can just return a ring mapping.
cues.zh: 所以一个选择是，你实际写代码去查看返回了什么并处理它，对吧？这仍然是 end class 的做法。不过我通常就是这么做的。原因在于，这通常其实并不太难，对吧？我反正倾向于检查这些东西，但你也可以决定不这么做。如果你愿意，你也可以直接返回一个环形映射。

cues.en: So similar to what happens when you call mmap on Linux where it just maps the same 4k page repeated like forever, right? So then you can just return a pointer to that page and people can read and write to it for the rest of time and they'll never crash, but they also didn't actually do anything.
cues.zh: 这类似于在 Linux 上调用 mmap 时发生的情况：它会把同一个 4k 页面无限重复地映射，对吧？于是你可以直接返回指向那个页面的指针，之后大家一直都能读写它，永远不会崩溃，但他们实际上也什么都没做成。

cues.en: So that's a good option if you really just want to go look. I want to handle any failure cases here but I also don't want to introduce any overhead into the code or possible mistakes because a lot of people are going to be using variable sized things and don't want them to have to test anything. That almost never happens. It's really rare because most things aren't variable sized. So that's why I usually just return a stub that you write to. But if it's really truly variable sized, right?
cues.zh: 所以如果你真的只是想先看看，那是个好选择。我想在这里处理任何失败情况，但我也不想给代码引入任何开销或可能的错误，因为很多人会使用可变大小的东西，而我不想让他们必须去测试任何东西。这种情况几乎从不发生。非常罕见，因为大多数东西都不是可变大小的。所以这就是为什么我通常只返回一个可以往里写的桩。但如果它真的确实是可变大小的，对吧？

cues.en: you can just return a repeat mapped page, which is a stub for arbitrary sizes, right? So you can do that if you want. So the way that I do stub stuff is I use what I call zero as initialization. So it's like RAII but good. Zero as initialization just means that memory is zero by default, which is true anyway. Any memory you get from the operating system is zero by default. You have to be like on an embedded system or something before that's not true.
cues.zh: 你可以直接返回一个重复映射页，这就是一个适用于任意大小的桩，对吧？所以你想的话可以这么做。我做桩相关东西的方式，是用我称为“零即初始化”的做法。它就像 RAII，但是更好。零即初始化只是说内存默认是零，反正本来也就是这样。你从操作系统拿到的任何内存默认都是零。只有像嵌入式系统之类的地方，这才不成立。

cues.en: But for security concerns on Windows, Mac, Linux, whatever, the memory you get back is zero. So the way that I handle stubs is all code is written so that zero is the default case, which means that you can always return a stub, which is just a block of zeros. So you just have a stub in memory that's a block of zeros, and anytime something fails, you just return that one instead. Then when the person actually reads to it or reads from it or writes from it, it just...
cues.zh: 但出于安全考虑，无论在 Windows、Mac 还是 Linux 上，你拿到的内存都会被清零。所以我处理桩代码的方式是，把所有代码都写成以零为默认情况，这意味着你总能返回一个全是零的存根。所以你在内存里放一个全零的存根，任何时候只要出错，直接返回它就行了。之后别人去读它或者写它时，它就……

cues.en: It doesn't do anything. And then at the end, you just clear it, right? At the end of the frame, you just clear it. Or every time you're going to go hand it out again, you clear it. No, the code doesn't check to see if the struct is a stub. It just assumes that the struct is something you can use and uses it, right? I do the same thing for like zero handles now. So like, for example, if you call get entity with the ID of zero these days, I don't return null. I just return
cues.zh: 它什么都不会做。然后在最后，你直接把它清零，对吧？在帧结束时把它清空。或者每次准备再次分发它之前清空一下。不，代码不会去检查这个结构体是不是存根。它直接默认这个结构体可用并直接使用，对吧？我现在对零句柄也是这么处理的。比如现在你要是调用 get entity 并传入 ID 为 0，我不会返回 null，而是直接返回

cues.en: a all zero entity. And then everyone just uses that. That's just what I do, right? I just find that it removes so much error handling and just kind of works pretty much. So that's just better. You just lose a lot of your handling code. It's nice. So I highly recommend ZII and stubs. It simplifies things tremendously. Handmade Hero doesn't use them very much because it's sort of something that I've only developed in the past couple of years.
cues.zh: 一个全零的实体。然后所有人直接用就行了。我就是这么干的，对吧？我发现这样省去了大量的错误处理逻辑，而且基本都能正常工作。这样显然更好。你可以砍掉大量的处理代码，非常爽。所以我强烈推荐零初始化（ZII）和存根。它极大地简化了一切。《Handmade Hero》里用得不多，因为这是我过去两三年才总结出来的方法。

cues.en: But, you know, I highly recommend it now. If I was doing Handmade Hero today, we would absolutely be ZII and Stubbs everywhere. In Handmade Hero, we still are to a certain extent, but not as much as we could be, right?
cues.zh: 但是，你知道的，我现在强烈推荐它。如果我今天重写《Handmade Hero》，我们绝对会到处使用 ZII 和存根。在《Handmade Hero》里我们在一定程度上确实用了，但远没有达到应有的程度，对吧？
